topic.title: BP Texas City, March 2005: the board said the splitter tower was nearly empty while it filled almost to the top, overflowed through its relief valves into a vent stack with no flare, and the vapour cloud ignited by the contractors' trailers

title: BP Texas City: The Gauge Said the Tower Was Nearly Empty
description:
BP's Texas City gauge said the tower was nearly empty. What was really inside it?
We rebuild the moment of failure in 3D from the U.S. Chemical Safety Board's report: the overfilled tower, the relief valves, the vent stack with no flare and the vapour cloud that reached the trailers.
The full minute-by-minute story is on the channel.
Sources: CSB (Mar 2007).
Based on official investigation reports and published sources. 3D scenes are reconstructions, not actual footage.
cta: Gauge or trailers: which should have stopped it? Comment

lines.text: At BP's Texas City, this gauge says it's draining.
Inside, it's 158 feet high, in a tower 170 feet tall. Where does it go?
Why can't the board see it? Its gauge reads only the bottom 9 feet.
It overflows, down a pipe, through relief valves, for 6 minutes.
They feed an old vent stack with no flare. It erupts like a geyser.
Vapour drifts toward the contractors' trailers, and a pickup truck idling nearby.
At 20 past 1, it finds a spark.
15 people died, all in or near those trailers.
Gauge or trailers: which should have stopped it? Full story on our channel. It happened

Disclaimer at end of description; deaths stated once, no gore; verify items (Eva Rowe, API RP 753) not used. Note: 'nearly empty' rests on Fig 6 (board indicated 7.9 ft of liquid in a 170-ft tower) while the transmitter itself read 78% of its 5-ft span, so never show a percent on the LOW readout; the truck spark is the report's 'most likely' source.

hook: 'this gauge reads low' is wrong on the gauge's own scale. CSB final report: at 1:04 p.m. the level transmitter read 78 percent (7.9 ft), above its 72 percent high-level alarm set point, which had already sounded at 3:09 a.m. (timeline; footnotes at the 72%/78% alarms). The gauge read HIGH in its range, not low; what it got wrong was the trend and the height (report: it 'indicated that the liquid level in the splitter tower was gradually declining, although it was actually rising'). Fix: say what the report says, e.g. 'At BP's Texas City, this gauge says the level is falling.' (or 'says it's draining'), and change the hook's LOW readout / 'THE GAUGE SAYS LOW' plate to match (e.g. a falling-level arrow), never a low reading or a percent.
